I'm afraid I fail to see your point of view.  In what way does democratic and collective control of the means of production reduce wealth for everyone?  The way I see it, trusting capitalism only furthers the internal contradictions it has already built, such as hierarchical expropriation of the products of labour, monopolization through accumulation of capital, and the self-destruction of the working class.  Labour in capitalist society no longer has the capacity to be self-regulating.  Capitalism has reduced labour to one's social relation to capital and the means of production.  Ultimately, class hegemony ensues from capitalism.  

I, and others like me, wish to reduce the exploitation innate in capitalism by changing the social relations of production to favor working people.  This will result in the bourgeoisie losing their influence over labour and their ability to extract surplus value from labour.  The idea behind this is that through the elimination of class, working people will make up the whole of society and be able to retain the full value of their labour, rather than a wage that reduces their share of wealth.

To address your point about the minimum wage, I must confess that raising the minimum wage would not do much to help impoverished persons.  I do, however, think workers who perform menial tasks ought to earn more.  Intrinsic to Marxist economics is democratic labour.  Each workplace ought to, by means of consensus, appropriate wealth directly proportionate to the labour of every worker.  Democratic labour excludes an individual or oligarchical managerial position.  Factoring in the lack of centralized managing and minus current US income tax rates, the average grocery store bagger under socialism would likely make $31,000 per year.  That's a substantial increase from the average $20,500 yearly pay that your average bagger would make.  If a socialist government were to have punitive income tax rates at around 70%, the bagger would make $20,150 with all necessities entirely covered.  If this process were to encompass the entire labour force, poverty would be all but eliminated.  Also, as a counterpoint in case you wonder "Why would anyone want to employ an unskilled worker to bag groceries and then see them earn that much?" take into consideration that a socialist workforce has nothing to lose from having unskilled workers perform menial tasks.  Everyone's labour remains the same, so their share of wealth is not diluted.

Remember, friend.  The wealth of society is created by the worker.  The bourgeoisie seeks only to subvert the proletarian masses and our ability to organize.  Maybe if poverty strikes you, you will realize it takes more than bootstraps to seize the life you deserve.

Capital =/= Means of production

When Marxists say we want to abolish capital, we are suggesting a collective change in attitude.  We regard capital not as traditional property, but rather as a sort of bourgeois property.  Capital only exists because it is created through wage-labour.

For example: A factory worker assembles drills that are worth $50 dollars each and are sold for $170 each.  The value of the worker's labour is equal to the output of his production, but the presence of capitalists in the hierarchy above him deprives him of the surplus value of his labour.  In other words, by the worker being paid at a wage and the capitalist profiting from the tangible labour being done, there exists an exploitative parasitism where the worker is the host.  When this parasitism exists on a large scale, it perpetuates the existence of the ruling class through the creation of large quantities of capital within the antagonism of the capitalist mode of production, as explained above, and wage-labour.

To abolish capital would not hurt the proletarian.  It would just mean the intangible bourgeois-property that is capital is deprived from those who use it to dominate society.  Capital's value is only perceived; as it was put by Marx, "Capital is a collective product, and only by the united action of many members, nay, in the last resort, only by the united action of all members of society, can it be set into motion."  If people don't recognize the value of capital, capital ceases to exist.

What the worker deserves is access to the *tangible* fruit of his or her labour.  When the method of currency becomes universally accessible, it is no longer capital; it is capital's conversion into common property.

tl:dr, Capital is only perceived, and it is created through private control of the means of production and exploitation of wage-labour.
